REFERENCE BY CHAIR 
Successful Launching of the CARTOSAT-1 and HAMSAT with PSLV from 
ISRO new launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I am sure all the hon. Members of this au gust e will join 
me in congratulating the Indian Space Re search isation of today's successful 
launch of the CARTOSAT-1 with PSLV. lunch took place form ISRO's new 
launch pad built at Satish Dhawan i Centre SHAR, Sriharikota, India's premier 
launch centre. This  pad is one of the most sophisticated in its capability and 
can meet ly the needs of the present generation of PSLV and GSLV but also 
more advanced versions to be built in the next decade and beyond. Successful 
launch of PSLV from this launch pad is a major milestone ICs plan to develop 
state-of-the-art infrastructure for conducting  launch operations. 
The primary satellite in this mission is a 1560 Kg state-of-the-art te sensing 
satellite CARTOSAT-1, carrying a camera sy stem to picture from space, that 
can delineate features to the level of 2.5  and in the forward and aft directions 
along the path of the satellite, a capability provides a unique method of 
producing three-isional details of the ground terrain. Among other things the 
various abilities include newer applications in the rural and urban opment, 
disaster assessment, relief planning and management, 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
environment impact assessment and various other geographical information 
system applications. The satellite is expected to pioneer a new era of 
mapping. 
CARTOSAT-1 joins the constellati on of Indian Remote Sensing 
Satellites, the largest in the civilian domain anywhere in the world. These 
satellites provide vital data on land and ocean resources hot only to meet the 
Indian needs but also of the global remote sensing community. This mission is 
expected to further strengthen Indi a's pre-eminent position among the handful 
of countries who design, launch and operate sate-of-the-art remote sensing 
satellites. 
A similar 42 kg satellite called HAMSAT was also placed in the orbit 
during this launch. HAMSAT is the Indian contribution to the international 
community of amateur radio operators. 
Alongwith all the hon. Members, I take this opportunity to warmly 
greet the entire ISRO community and also other organisations, both public 
and private which were closely associated with ISRO in the realisation of this 
important mission. The entire country lauds them for this singular 
achievement. 
THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, 1 share the nation's sense of delight and pride at the news that 
we have received from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. Sir, you 
have already mentioned the successful launch of the PSLV-C6 carrying 
CARTOSAT-1 and HAMSAT payloads this morning from the second launch 
pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre in the presence of the hon. President of 
India. This is indeed yet another si gnificant milestone in the Indian space 
programme. The state-of-the-art second launch pad, which the President 
dedicated to the nation this morning, augments our launch capabilities 
considerably and reaffirms once again the emergence of India as a major 
space power. Space, technology and ap plications have become a very 
significant part of our scientific and development capabilities. The launch of 
CARTOSAT-1 will herald a new era in advanced remote sensing 
applications. The launch of the smaller HAMSAT will be a welcome 
resource for the community of amateur ra dio enthusiasts. Sir, the nation is 
truly proud of the achievement of our dedicated scientists and engineers of 
the Indian Space Research Organisation. I am sure all hon. Members will join 
me and join you in congratulating our scientists and technologists and 
wishing them still greater success in the years to come.

Re. Request to Persuade Opposition Leaders to Participate in 
the Proceedings of Parliament 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY(Andhra Pradesh): Sir, 
we have not been attending the House for the past few days. This is due to the 
casual attitude of the Government towards the Opposition. The vindictive 
attitude of the UPA Government has forced the Opposition to boycott the 
Parliamentary proceedings. Sir, the attitude of UPA Government towards the 
Opposition is most deplorable. The st atements of some leaders of the 
Congress Party have also contributed to this unfortunate episode. Neither the 
Prime Minister nor the Parliamentary Af fairs Minister tried to resolve the 
issue. For a health democracy the role of the Opposition is very important. 
The UPA Government is ignoring this aspect. We have boycotted the 
proceedings on a principle and we thought that the Government would come 
forward and resolve the issue. On the one hand, the Government is not 
willing to have a dialogue with the Opposition; and, on the other hand, they 
are trying to further precipitate the issu e. Sir, the people of our country will 
take note of this casual attitude of the Government towards the Opposition. 
While condemning the attitude of the Government, we would like to 
participate in the proceedings of the Pa rliament under protest. Even now the 
hon Prime Minister can resolve the issue by inviting the Opposition and 
persuade them to participate in the proceedings in the larger interest of the 
nation and parliamentary democracy. 
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 581 
Cheating by Authorised PCO booth owners 
*581. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  a large number of authorised 
PCO booth owners in Delhi are cheating the PCO users for local calls by 
manipulating the timing device; 
(b) if so, whether any surprise checks are conducted to ensure that PCO 
owners do not indulge in such irregularities; and 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
(c) if so, in what manner and if not, why? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) to (c) A statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Cheating by Authorised PCO Booth Owners  
(a) Yes, Sir. Complaints on local PCOs for overcharging are received 
from time to time. The Complaints are mainly towards charging of Rs. 21- 
by PCO owners instead of normal charge of Re. 1/- for 90 seconds pulse 
which has since been revised to Rs. 21- for 120 seconds pulse with effect 
from 01.04.2005 in MTNL, Delhi. No tampering of timing device for local 
calls have been reported in MTNL, Delhi. 
(b) Yes, Sir. Periodic/surprise checks are carried out by the staff and 
the Vigilance Cell besides entertaining consumer complaints. 
(c) Sir, normally, a 16 Khz pulse is sent to the STD PCOs to operate 
the charging devise, installed at STD PCO location. For local calls, timing 
device is used by the PCO operator to disconnect/extend the call after 
stipulated period. 
During checks, calls are made posi ng as customer to ascertain the 
correctness of charging. If any irregularities are noticed, warning and notice 
is given to the PCO owner for correctiv e action. In case of repeated/ serious 
complaints, the PCO is disconnected permanently. 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is a large network of PCO 
booths. Most PCO booths also have ISD and STD facilities. Whereas the rates 
for ISD and STD calls over the years have been reduced, the rates and pulse of 
the local PCO calls have registered appr eciable changes over the years. In the 
event of the changes of pulses, it is the responsibility of the MTNL staff to 
make adjustments in the machines, which they hardly do leaving the job to 
booth owners to make or not to make the changes as they like, while charging 
the revised higher rates. The rates are hardly displayed in the booths. 
However, when the MTNL staff make changes in the machines the booth 
owners tamper to adjust the pulse for th eir benefit. The present rate of pulse 
for two minutes is for 120 seconds is Rs. 2/- where earlier... 
4 

[5 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put your question. 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Sir, the question is that the hon. Minister has 
already in his reply said very clearly that this process and this thing do 
happen. But he has not said and I would like to know from him how many 
complaints have come to him and what is the action he has taken so far 
against them? 
SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN: Sir, I would like to tell the hon. 
Member that last year alone 7151 surp rise checks were done in all the PCOs 
throughout the country. Sir, we have taken actions against all the PCOs which 
were having faulty meters, or, not displaying the tariffs. It is an on-going 
process. We are continuously monitoring it. 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Sir, my second supplementary is this. Whether it 
is true that there is no provision in  the contract between the BSNL/ MTNL 
and the PCO booth owners for imposing penalty or taking any legal action, 
or, even terminating the agreement on this particular issue. 
SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN: Sir, I would like to inform the hon. 
Member that most of the pulse rate s are set at the exchange for PCOs. 
Whenever we find that they are not fo llowing the prescribed norms, we take 
action against them. If it is found that they have faulty meters and are wilfully 
engaging themselves in unlawful prac tices, we cancel and terminate their 
licences. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, major irregularities are reported in the case 
of private service providers for basic te lephone services and cellular services. 
So, I would like to know from the hon. Minister as to what are the major 
irregularities that have been reported from various parts of the country. Who 
are the top-ranking private service prov iders liable for this? What are all the 
extra efforts/all out efforts the Ministry is taking? The hon. Minister is saying 
that he is doing this and that. They are always there. The Department is in 
existence for several decades now and th e system is also in existence since 
decades. I would like to know what extra efforts the Ministry is taking to plug 
this kind of lapses. 
SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN: Sir, basically, I hope the hon. Member's 
question is relating to PCOs, not a general one. If it is relating to PCOs, as I 
explained earlier, we can do this only through surprise checks. Majority of 
the PCOs are run by the BSNL in the country and by the MTNL in Delhi

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
& Mumbai. Now, even private operators are offering PCO services to public. 
Earlier there were complaints that, when the local call rate was Re. 1 for 90 
seconds pulse, the PCOs were overchar ging the customer by collecting Rs. 2 
and not returning the balance. So, to avoid this, both, the BSNL and the 
MTNL Delhi have decided to increase th e local call charge to Rs. 2 with a 
pulse of 120 seconds. The idea behind is  that the customer gets due value for 
his money and PCOs will not overcharge. We also give more incentives to 
PCOs. We are also increasing their co mmission to ensure that PCOs do not 
try to fleece customers. Sir, specific co mplaints are very rare. Most of the 
complaints are attended to by the Department or the operators when they go 
on check. If there is any specific compla int, instead of a general one, I assure 
the hon. Member that the Department will definitely take action, because it 
becomes easy for us to perform our duty.

Exploration of Space 
*583. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what new projects are being plan ned for the exploration of Space 
during the next three years; 
(b) whether there is any project to se nd a man to Space, if not, the 
reasons therefor; 
6 

[5 May, 2005]  RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether Government are satisfied with the progress made by Indian 
Scientists in the field of Space exploration and technology; and 
(d) if so, the progress made to justify the money spent in this field? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
Exploration of Space 
(a) Two new projects are planned for the exploration of s,pace during 
the next three years. They ar e CHANDRAYAAN-1 and ASTROSAT 
missions. Chandrayaan-1 is the first Indian unmanned mission to the Moon 
meant for the exploration of lunar su rface and mineralogy. ASTROSAT is a 
multi-wavelength astronomical observ atory in space for studies of the 
phenomena of variability in different types of stellar objects simultaneously 
covering a range of high-energy radiations from X-rays and gamma rays to 
far/hear Ultraviolet (UV) along with observations in visible part of the 
spectrum. 
(b) No, Sir. Manned space missions are not envisaged at the present 
juncture to meet the primary objectiv e of Indian space programme,, which is 
to achieve self reliance in development of satellites and launch vehicles 
technology and to utilise space technol ogy for application programmes in 
communications and earth observation besi des societal applications such as 
tele-education, tele-medicine, meteorology, disaster management support etc. 
The present status of advancement in space technology makes it possible to 
meet the above objectives using unmanned spacecraft. Also, the cost 
associated with manned missions is an order of magnitude higher and, at 
'present, the gains expected from such missions do not justify high 
investments. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) Today IRS system with six spacecra ft in orbit is providing multi 
spectral high-resolution imageries for various applications of resource survey 
and management on operational basis. The INSAT system of eight satellites in 
operation with about 150 transponders is providing operational services for 
broadcasting, television, communications and meteorological observations in 
addition to societal applications i such as 
7 

RAJYA SABHA  [5 May, 2005] 
tele-medicine, tele-education'. Two launch vehicles namely PSLV and GSLV 
have been indigenously designed and developed for meeting the operational 
launch services of all IRS and two tonne class INSAT/GSAT satellites. 
Today, India is one among six nations in the world possessing the capability 
to build geostationary satellites and la unch them into sp ace with their own 
launch vehicle. 
Money spent in this area has been effectively utilized in building the 
infrastructure, design and development of the above space systems in addition 
to delivery of the operational system s. The self-reliance achieved in 
technology and the successful application programmes besides the 
commercial gains in communication and remote sensing areas more than 
outweigh the investments made so far.

SHRI V. NARAYANASAMI: Hon. Chairman, Sir, our scientists, by 
launching the satellite today, have proved that they are doing a very good job 
in the field of space research. It is a landmark in space research. The hon. 
Minister, in his reply, has mentioned that there is no programme for sending a 
man to the space. The United States ha s done it and other countries are also 
attempting to do it. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether the 
Government is thinking of  sending a man to the space in future, say, after 9-
10 years. The second part of my question is, some other countries have also 
manufactured their spacecrafts and satellite s, but they do not have launching 
pads. Some countries, like the United St ates, are providing their launching 
pads for use to the countries, like Japan, China and such other countries. I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether India is also going to 
provide its launching pad for use by such countries. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir. as I said, the CHANDRAYAAN-
1 Mission is a moon observation mission. It is not a manned mission at all. 
We have no plan to send a man to the moon, as of now, because we think the 
expenses will not be in commensurate with benefits. 
As far as the second part of the question is concerned, India has already 
offered its launch capabilities to all the countries that want to launch their 
own satellite. We are offering to take payloads of some countries. We have 
already got projects to take satellites from some of our friendly countries. We 
have a special cooperation, the antriksha cooperation, which is specifically 
doing the job of marketing the Indian launch vehicle capabilities to other 
countries that want to launch their own satellites. 
PROF. P.J. KURIAN: Sir, the hon. Minister, in his reply, has said that 
a manned space flight is not contempl ated because the expenditure is not 
commensurate with the gains. What I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister is, how does he calculate gains with regard to a manned space 
flight? Is it simply on monetary terms? Sir, sending a man to the space is a 
matter of pride for the nation. Today, we have achieved such a great success. 
The ISRO scientists have got acclamation not only from India, but also from 
all over the world. 
10 

[5 May, 2005]  RAJYA SABHA 
Therefore, the gains from a manned space flight should be calculated in 
the form of pride and the international repute that we will be achieving. In 
view of that, I would like to know whether the hon. Prime Minister will 
reconsider the question of not contemplating a manned space flight, and will 
also examine whether a manned space flight  is possible. I know it is possible 
for our scientists. Why does he not plan for a manned space flight? I would 
like the hon. Prime Minister to answer this question. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, these Chandrayan and Astrosat 
experiments are in the areas of space science. We already have other series of 
satellites for remote sensing and for communication. So, we are now 
attempting to gain capability in deep space communication, deep launch 
capability, precise navigation, and all that. It is not that we have ruled out, at 
a future date, a man mission. All I said was, at this stage, we are not 
contemplating a man mission. 
SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, will the Prime Minister 
inform the House of any plan of Space Department to enhance the capacity of 
the Sriharikota Station, which is rendering an excellent service in this field? I 
want to know how many countries, including the payload countries, have so 
far utilised our launching pad in Sriharikota. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, the Satish Dhavan Space Centre 
in Sriharikota, from where the satellite was launched today, is a world-class 
facility. Only yesterday, our hon. Rash trapatiji dedicated the second launch 
site in the Sriharikota complex. So , the Sriharikota complex is being 
expanded. At the moment, no foreign satellite has been launched from India. 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, whilst re joicing in the achievements of 
our space scientists, I would like to put to the hon. Minister a very simple 
question about the utilisation of all the capabilities that we are developing. 
Specifically, we have developed remote sensing satellites and we have 
launched an Edusat. On the ground, how are these being utilised? Is the 
information from these satellites being actually utilised? Other than signing 
MOUs between ISRO and the various State Governments, what do we have 
to show for it? 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, I think, the achievements of ISRO 
and the Department of Space are enviable. We are one of the largest

countries in the world with the largest capabilities. We have seven space 
aircraft as of now. ...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: That is not my question. 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: I am coming to that. By monitoring 
Earth observation and India observation, we are getting very high quality 
maps of India, high resolution maps of our terrain, and other countries, which 
are being sold commercially. They are being used very effectively in planning 
our being sold commercially. We have got eight communication satellites. 
We have 150 transponders. So, we should be proud of this achievement. All 
the telecommunication that we have an d the television programmes that are 
being broadcast are using this satellite. The Earth observation role is a very 
important role. There is the Natural Resource Management System. The 
backbone of that System is our IRS Satellites. And we are doing a very good

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: I would like to know from the hon. Minister

with the European Space Ag ency to assist in our Space Based Navigation

national security scenario? 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, we are discussing and 
participating in the GALILEO Progra mme, which is a Satellite Navigation 
Programme. I think, the collaboration in th is field will, definitely, go further. 
We are playing a very important role along with the European Space Agency 
to participate in this programme. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr Anand Sharma. This is the last supplementary. 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Thank you, Sir. Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is a 
very proud day for the country as you and the hon. Prime Minister have

informed about the satellites and also their capabilities. I would like to know 
(a) whether India is prepared to share the data, which we are collecting, with 
the developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America to help them, not 
commercially, but as a gift to those who are looking upto us. And secondly, at 
what stage is the utilisation of the ED USAT, which was gifted by the hon. 
President to the African continent and what are the results?

of COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of electronic telephone exchange set up in Tamil Nadu 
during the last three years; 
(b) the details of the electronic telephone exchanges proposed to be set 
up during 2005-06; and 
(c) the details of the other steps being taken to improve the 
communication facility in Tamil Nadu? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) to (c): A statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Setting Electronic Telephone Exchanges in Tamil Nadu 
(a) The details of electronic telephon e exchanges set up in Tamil Nadu 
during the last three years is given in  Statement I, II & III respectively (See 
below) 
(b) The details of electronic telephone exchanges proposed to be set up 
during 2005-06 is given in statement IV (See below) 
(c) The details of other steps being taken to improve the 
communication facility in Tamil Nadu are as follows: 
(i) Introduction of more RSUs (Remote Switching Units)/DLCs 
(Digital Loop Carrier) to reduce the cable length resulting in 
reduction of faults due to cables. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
(ii) Up-gradation of external plant including poleless activity to 
improve the performance of outdoor network,  
(iii) Replacement of fault prone paper core U/G cables  
(iv) Addition of DLCs (Digital loop carriers) to reduce the last mile 
problems and to meet high speed data circuit requirements,  
(v) Introduction of Wireless in local loop (WLL) system to cover 
larger rural areas,  
(vi) Provision of Interactive Voice Response System (IVRS) 
based centralized fault booking at SDCC's (Short Distance 
Charging Centre)/LDCC (Long Distance Charging Centre),  
(vii) Conversion of C-DOT 256 exchanges into AN RAXs (Access 
Network Rural Automatic Exchanges),  
(viii) Conversion of SBM (Single Base Module) Exchanges into 
RSU Exchanges,  
(ix) Provision of maintenance free battery sets and Engine 
Alternator for backup power supplies,  
(x) Entering into annual- maintenance contract for New 
Technology switches and for WLL switches including FWTs 
(Fixed Wireless terminals)  
(xi) Provision of high capacity external maintenance free batteries 
with FWT for longer talk time & standby time. 
(xii) Addition of mobile switching capacity in the towns wherever 
needed. 
(xiii) Extending/im proving the coverage of existing mobile services 
in terms of higher indoor/in-signal levels. 
(xiv) Improvement of mobile network of highways to provide rural 
coverage to the enroute towns/villages.

Loans given by KVIC 
*586. SHRI R.K.ANAND: Will the Minister of AGRO AND RURAL 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that KVIC con tinued to release rebate claim and 
extend financial assistance to the tune  of about Rs. 4 crores as loan to 
institutions in violation of its own rules; and 
(b) the steps taken by Government for the protection of artisans rights? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRO A ND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHABIR PRASAD): (a) and (b) A Statem ent is placed on the Table of the 
Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) The Khadl Certification Rules and the Khadi Certification Code, 
2003 provide for the creation of Artisan  Welfare Fund (AWF) at the level of 
each institution registered with the Kh adi and Village Industries Commission 
(KVIC) for the welfare of the self-employed artisans who supply khadi 
articles to the institution. Artisans' subscriptions and matching contributions 
of the institutions at such rates as may be prescribed by the Central 
Certification Committee or the KVIC or its authorised officers are deposited 
into the AWF. In case of default in this respect by an institution, various 
corrective measures have been provided for, which include not paying the 
rebate amounts to the institutions concerned. 
However, the KVIC has released the rebate amounts to the Khadi 
institutions which did not fully comply with the above-mentioned provisions 
regarding the AWF. The rebate amounts were released to these Khadi 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
institutions to enable  them to buy and supply n ecessary raw materials to the 
Khadi, artisans, buy yarn and supply  it to the artisans (weavers) and pay 
wages to the artisans. If the rebate amounts were not released to these 
institutions, the difficulties of the artis ans on account of loss of employment 
and wages would have increased further. The KVIC has, however, stopped 
providing financial assistance in the form of loan to its registered institutions 
since 1997-98. 
(b) As a measure of providing social  security to the khadi artisans, 
Janashree Bima Yojana (JBY) has been launched with effect from 15 August, 
2003 to cover 3.9 lakh artisans during the remaining period of the 10th Plan. 
The scheme provides for insurance cove rage against death and disability to 
khadi artisans. 2.03 lakh artisans have been covered under this scheme up to 
31 January, 2005. 
SHRI R.K. ANAND: Mr. Chairman, Sir,  for the benefit of artisans, the 
codified rules lay down the creation of  Artisan Welfare Fund which consists 
of 10 per cent of the artisan wages and an equal matching by the institutions 
employing them. This is to be deposited in nationalised banks. I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister as to how many institutions are not depositing 
this amount collected from the employees and the matching contribution by 
them in the bank.

The State Governments are the approp riate authority for ensuring the

Act, 1948. Accordingly, monitoring of the implementation of minimum 
wages in respect of beedi workers is done by the respective State 
Governments. 
Deduction of employees' contribution and remittance thereof along

for all establishments (including Beedi Establishments) under the

31.3.2004, 17.96 lakh beedi workers in respect of 4158 establishments were

THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. TRAI 
has laid down the QoS parameters applicable for Basic and Cellular Mobile 
Service Provider's network vide gazette notification No. 112-17/98-TRAI

(c) The QoS parameters for basic se rvice are applicable to both 
wireline and wireless. However, as per the report received by TRAI,

December, 2004, BSNL and MTNL are not meeting the stipulated 
benchmarks of TRAI, in respect of certain parameters. MTNL and BSNL

very old and fault prone. Almost one-third of the telecom lines and about 
79% of telephone exchange of BSNL are working in rural, far flung and 
difficult to access areas where there is either no power or reliable electric 
supply. Further, in fast developing scenario, some areas become technically 
non-feasible. The two PSUS are continously taking measures to meet the 
service parameters by modernizing the network, providing innovative

Review of Central Schemes 
*592. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any national review wa s undertaken on the performance/ 
implementation of Central Schemes/Programmes; 
(b) if so, the detals thereof including findings thereof and the steps 
being taken/proposed to be taken thereon; 
(c) whether it is a fact that most of the development/welfare schemes 
were unable to reach the target bene ficiaries due to embezzlement in the 
middle; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the steps proposed to be taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The implementing Ministries regularly 
undertake Review of implementation of their Programmes. Planning 
Commission too has introduced a system of Quarterly Progress Review 
(QPR) Meetings of Central Plan Schemes. In addition, Programme 
Evaluation Organization (PEO), Planning Commission undertakes Evaluation 
of some selected Central Plan Schemes. 
(b) Subejct Divisions of the Planning Commission have undertaken a 
number of QPR meetings covering various Sectors. In addition, PEO has 
conducted 175 Evaluation Studies si nce its inception. Findings and 
suggestions of recently evaluated sc hemes are given in Statement-I (See 
below). The implementing Central Ministries/Deptts.as well as the State 
Governments also get evaluation studies conducted by Research Institutes & 
NGOs. 
(c) However, the Government is aware that there is scope for 
improvement in the delivery system. The findings of evaluation studies 
conducted by PEO tend to suggest that the intended benefits of some 
developmental/welfare schemes are not reaching the targeted pupulation to 
the desired extent. 
(d) The findings and suggestions are communicated to the 
concerned ministries/subject divisions of the Planning Commission for 
56 

[5 May, 2005]  RAJYA SABHA 
mid-course corrections and restructuring of schemes/programmes. From 
information gathered, some of the Ministries have taken action on PEO 
reports, which is given in Statement-ll. 
Statement I 
Findings and Suggstions of recently evaluated schemes 
(i) Khadi and Village Industries Programme 
The findings of the study shows that inadequate linkage between 
production and sales strategies has resulted in accumulation of stocks, low 
return on investment, non-performing asset build-up, low production and 
shrinking employment opportunities. The budgetary support has come down 
considerably with the introduction of MMS (Margin Money Scheme). The 
study reveals that another area of concern is the high raw material to output 
ratio. Due to part-time employment in khadi sector, the income of workers is 
low compared to village industries workers. Many poor households actually 
crossed the poverty line with the help of additional income from the KVIC 
programme. 
(ii) Scoial Safety Net Programmes (SSNP) 
. The main findings of the study reveal that the programme suffers 
largely due to the lack of proper infrastructure facilities. The other factors 
such as post of lady doctor, the absenteeism among the doctors from their 
work places, behaviour of para-medical  & auxiliary para-medical staff has 
worsened the situation. The beneficiaries are dissatisfied with the functioning 
of PHCs. The main reasons for the low income group households to stay 
away from the public health care deliver y system are the non-availability of 
medicine, indirect cost on transport and high opportunity cost in terms of 
foregone income (due to loss of wage income say). 
(iii) Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) 
The impact of the scheme as felt by the local people indicate that about 
65% of the created assets have been rated as good and overwhelming 
majority of them have opined that the created assets are as per the felt needs 
and has improved their quality of life. The study reveals softie major flaws in 
the implementation such as preference for roads & bridges and community 
works, meager allocation in spite of large 
57 

RAJYA SABHA  [5 May, 2005] 
unspent balance, weak monitoring and supervision and lack of maintenance. 
The study suggests that there is a need for revitalizing the scheme in terms of 
financial management, inter-departmental coordination for implementation 
and involvement of PRIs for identifying the proper works, monitoring and 
maintenance of the created assets. 
(iv) Evaluation Study of the National Project on Bio-gas Development 
The study reveals the percentage of plants in working condition is very 
low and sanitary linked plants have  a lower acceptability due to socio-
psychological inhibitions in respect of routine operation of these plants. Most 
State level biogas cells are overstaffed, while in districts, staff deficiency was 
felt. The household demand for family type biogas plants is influenced by 
factors like availability of alternate convenient fuels (LPG), distance of a 
village from the nearest town and inconvenience in handling and maintaining 
biogas plants. As for the community biogas plants, the MNES has almost 
discontinued the promotion of community biogas plants in the past five years. 
(v) Statutory Development Boards (SDBs) in Maharashtra 
The findings of the Stud y clearly indicate that not only did the Boards 
discharge their assigned functions and responsibilities reasonably well, but 
they also have brought about important changes in the planning process of 
Maharashtra for balanced regional development. However, the role played by 
the Governor's Office as an arbiter and in directing the activities of the 
Boards towards constructive purposes has been a very critical input towards 
this achievement. Also, subjecting the activites of the Boards to normal 
administrative procedures has helped the Boards in discharging their 
responsibilities efficiently and objectively. Therefore, the purpose of 
constituting the Boards for moderating and defusing sociopolitical tensions 
arising out of unacceptably large gaps  in the level of development across 
regions has, by and large, been fulfilled. PEO has suggested for continuance 
of the Boards beyond 2004 with their redefined role. 
(vi) Integrated Dairy Development Project (IDDP) 
The findings of the study tend to su ggest that except for a few isolated 
cases, the objectives of IDDP have not been realized. The areas of weakness 
in the scheme relate to several aspects of planning and 
58 

[5 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
implementation. The Dairy Cooperative Societies (DCSs) is the linchpin of 
IDDP and its viability, sustainability and effectiveness are crucial to the 
success of the scheme. For their viability  and effectiveness, the activities of 
DCSs should not remain confined to just procurement of milk, but be 
oriented to raise local milk production and marketable surplus. The DCSs 
should be geared to pr ovide a package of servi ces, which include Fodder 
Delivery, Veterinary Services, Awareness Generation and Capacity Building. 
Statement - II 
Action Taken in PEO Reports 
Action taken note on findings and su ggestions of recently conducted 
evaluation studies 
PEO has been undertaking studies only at the requests of various 
Ministries/Departments and Divisions of Planning Commission. The 
implementation of the findings and suggestion made in the evaluation reports 
brought out by PEO rests with the concerned Ministries/ Departments. It has 
been gathered that the findings and suggestions of PEO evaluation reports 
have been incorporated in vary ing degrees by the implementing 
Ministries/Departments. 
- Based on the evaluation report of PEO on Mahila Samriddhi 
Yojana, the scheme was abolished. 
-- The Employment Assurance Scheme was thoroughly restructured 
during 2001-02 and the detailed guidelines for the restructured scheme 
(Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana - SGRY) were issued in April, 2002 
which incorporated many of the recommendations of the report by PEO 
released in April, 2000. 
- The evaluation study, of Non-Formal Education Programme was 
taken up by PEO in the year 1997 and based on the recommendations of the 
PEO report the scheme was completely revamped and amalgamated in the 
new scheme entitled Education Guarantee Scheme and Alternative & 
Innovative Education (EGS & AIE). 
- The evaluation of National Project on Biogas Development (NPBD) 
was taken up by PEO in 2001 and based on the observations and 
recommendations of the evaluation report; the Ministry of 
59

Non-Conventional Resources formulated detailed guidelines for 
implementation of the programme during the year 2002-03 onwards. 
- The performance evaluation of Statutory Development Boards in 
Maharashtra was taken up by PEO and the report was released in April, 
2003. The findings and observations of PEO report were acknowledged 
by office of the Governor, Maharashtra and the three development boards 
of Marathawara, rest of Maharashtra and Vidharbha. 
~ The evaluation reports on A ccelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP), Functioning of Community Health Centres (CHCs),

† 598* SHRI MOTILAL VORA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYANA RAO): (a) to (c) Section 9 (3) of the Mines & 
Minerals (Development & Regulation), Act 1957 empowers the Central

friendly consultations and proceeding from the overa ll interests of bilateral 
relations. The two Prime Ministers expressed satisfaction over the progress 
made in the discussions between the Special Representatives on the boundry

clarification and confirmation of the line of actual control through the

Implementation of Confidence Building Measures in the Military Field along 
the Line of Actual Control in the India-China Border Areas" was also 
concluded.

Sale of Coal from Captive Mines to nearest PSUs 
4498. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government  have approved the sale of coal 
from captive mines to the nearest Public Sector Undertakings; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that Coal  Mines (Nationalization) Act does 
not allow sale of captive mining by private companies; and 
(c) if so, in what manner Government propose to sell coal from captive 
mines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYANA RAO): (a) It has been decided that coal produced 
from a captive mine during the development period of the mine may be 
transferred to the subsidiary coal company of Coal India Limited operating in 
the area at a price to be determined by a Committee under the Chairmanship 
of the Additional Secretary (Coal). 
(b) The Coal Mines (Nationalization) Act, 1973 is not a statute 
governing trade in coal. It determines the eligibility of a company to do 
mining of coal. The Act allows inter-alia, mining of coal by an Indian 
company for specified end uses only. 
(c) During the development phase of a captive mine, by when the end 
use plant may not be installed, the Government has allowed transfer of coal 
extracted from the captive mine to the local nati onalized coal company. This 
arrangement became necessary in order to avoid the hazards of storing coal 
for long period which leads to auto combustion and the adverse impact on the 
economy. In order to ensure that such tr ansfer does not turn into a trade by a 
private company, the Committee under th e Chairmanship of the Additional 
Secretary (Coal) has been constituted to determine the price at which coal 
will be transferred from captive mining to a Coal India subsidiary.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Planning 
Commission has suggested some critical initiatives for the development of 
coal sector which, inter-alia, include the following: 
(i) Expedite passing of Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 
2000 which would permit private sector in non-captive mining in 
order to augment domestic coal production for meeting the rising 
coal demand. 
(ii) Amend the provision of Mines and Minerals Development and 
Regulation (MMDR) Act, 1957 to fac ilitate offering of coal blocks 
to potential entrepreneurs on competitive bidding basis. 
(iii) Enlarge the scope of captive mining by permitting captive block 
holders to sell incidental coal production during development of the 
block at least to Coal India Ltd. (CIL). 
(iv) Restructure Coal India Ltd. (CIL) by doing away with the holding 
company structure and extending autonomy to individual coal 
producing companies for promoting competition amongst the 
national coal companies. 
(v) Permit trading of coal by removing it from the list of essential 
commodities. 
(vi) Change grading and pricing of non-coking coal from the existing 
Useful Heat Value (UHV) to Gr oss Calorific Value (GCV) to 
encourage efficient use and alloca tion and promote use of washed 
coal. 
(vii) Amend the provisions of Contract Labour (Regulation and 
Abolition) Act, 1970 to facilitate offloading of certain activities in 
coal mining for improved economics of operations. 
94 

[5 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) As a step towards abolishing coal linkages these linkages may be 
made tradable by power plants. 
The decisions/actions taken by the Government in respect of the above 
suggestions of the Planning Commission are as under: 
(i) The Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 2000 has been 
introduced in Rajya Sabha in April, 2000 to permit private 
participation in non-captive coal mining in order to augment coal 
production in the country. 
(ii) A proposal to amend the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 to 
allow allocation of coal blocks on competitive bidding basis is under 
consideration of the Government. 
(iii) Government has decided to enlarge the scope of captive mining by 
permitting captive holders to sell incidental coal production during 
the development of a mine to CIL.

Security Council seat without Veto-Powers 
4536. DR. AKHILESH DAS: 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any fresh proposals for expansion of the UN 
Security Council by induction of a few permanent and non-permanent 
members of the council, without Veto-Power; and 
(b) if so, the details of the proposals and whether India agreed to 
accept permanent membership of the Security Council without Veto Powers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) and (b) The issue of the reform and 
restructuring of the UN Security Council has been under discussion at the 
United Nations for several years. In view of the complexities and the diverse 
perceptions on the specifics of such reforms among member States, a 
decision on this issue has not been reached as yet. The High Level Panel on 
Threats, Challenges and Change' established by the UN Secretary General, in 
its report, released in December 2004, recognized the need for expansion of 
the UN Security Council, but, stopped short of making a definitive 
recommendation on new permanent members. Instead, it proposed two 
models 'A' and 'B' and recommended that "under any reform proposal, there 
should be no expansion of the Veto". Model 'A' provides for expansion in 
both the permanent and non-permanent 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
categories whereas Model 'B' envisages an additional non-permanent seat as 
well as creation of a new non-permanent category for a longer term tenure. It 
may be mentioned that the High Level Panel was Panel of independent 
experts and not an inter-Governmental body. The UN Secretary General in 
his report titled "In larger freedom: towards security, development and human 
rights for all" released on March 21, 2005 has urged Member States to 
consider the two options, models A and B, proposed in the report of the High 
Level Panel, or any other viable proposals in terms of size and balance that 
have emerged on the basis of either model. Discussions on this issue are 
underway in the UN. It is now for the UN members to take forward this 
process and to reach a d ecision. Regarding India's position on the issue of 
veto, Hon'ble Prime Minister has stated our position on the membership of 
the UN Security Council in the Parliament, which is that "there is no 
confusion regarding our position on our candidature for a Permanent Seat on 
the Security Council. At this point, all Permanent Members have veto powers. 
We are a candidate. This issue may arise in respect of any new Permanent 
Members who may be admitted. Our fundamental position remains clear. We 
do not believe there should be any discrimination in the Security Council and 
there should be no distinction between Permanent Members who have the 
veto and those who don't."

Hostage policy 
4546. SHRI RAJKUMAR  DHOOT: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Govern ment are working out a policy on 
hostages on the lines of Us-lsrael policy in this regrard; 
(b) if so, the details thereof along with main features of the policy; and 
(c) by when the policy is likely to be finalized and implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) It is the policy of the 
Government of India not to compromise with terrorist groups or elements. 
However, while adhering to this principle, the objective of the Government is 
to ensure the safety and well-being of all its citizens, whether in India or 
abroad. In case of hostage-taking, Government makes all efforts possible to 
secure the early and safe release of its nationals. In order to deal with 
144 

[5 May, 2005]  RAJYA SABHA 
hostage situations, a Crisis Management Group is set up immediately which 
is tasked with the constant monitoring and handling of the situation in close 
consultation with concerned agencies, our diplomatic missions abroad and 
with foreign governments. The Cabinet Secretary also holds a parallel set of 
inter-ministerial meetings, as required, to take appropriate decision. The 
Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs may also meet, as necessary, to 
review the situation and take appropri ate decisions. This mechanism remains 
in force until the crisis ends. It needs to be pointed out that no two hostage 
situations are entirely similar and different responses may be required 
depending upon specific circumstances to reach the objectives of Government 
policy.

4554. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA:

state: 
(a) whether despite legal provision, the child labour are being exploited 
on a large scale throughout the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, 
(c) whether Government's attention has been drawn to this by I.L.O. 
and if so, the details thereof; and 
 
151 

RAJYA SABHA  [5 May, 2005] 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken against persons responsible for 
violation of labour laws and save children from harassment? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRASEKHAR RAO): (a) and (b) Child Labour is a socioeconomic 
problem in the country. The Government  is committed to eliminate all forms 
of Child Labour through intervention under the NCLP scheme. Action is 
taken under the Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act wherever such 
cases are seem to occur. 
(c) I.L.O. is working in coordination with Government of India in its 
endeavour to eliminate all forms of child labour. 
(d) The Government is vigilant on the issue of the exploitation of child 
labour in the country and all out efforts are being made to withdraw such 
children from work for their rehab ilitation and to prosecute the erring 
employers. The State Governments are the appropriate Government for the 
implementation of Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986. 
Sufficient deterrent provisions have already been made in the said Act for 
persons violating the provisions of the Act. The Act provides that any person 
who employs any child in contravention of the provisions of the Act, is liable 
for punishment with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 
three months but which may extend to one year or with fine which shall not be 
less than Rs. 10,000 but which may extend to Rs. 20,000 or both. In order to 
eliminate child labour in all forms, Government has formulated a National 
Child Labour Project (NCLP) Sche me. Under the Scheme, the working 
children are withdrawn from work and put into special schools with the 
objective to mainstream them into formal system of education. The Scheme, 
which was initially started in 1988 with 12 districts in the country, has been 
expanded to cover 250 districts across 21 States during the Tenth Plan.

Concept of Poverty Line 
4584. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS K AUR: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that while incidence of poverty from 1977-78 to 
1999-2000 declined from 51.3 per cent to 25.1 per cent, the decline in 
number of persons below poverty line in absolute terms was not so marked, 
having come down from 328.9 million to 260.3 million; 
(b) if so, in what way the concept of poverty  line has undergone a 
change and the growth of population has come down during that period; and 
(c) the targets fixed for the Tenth Five  Year Plan with regard to the 
incidence of poverty and the number of people below poverty line and how 
far the same have been achieved by the end of 2004-05? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) Yes, Sir. It is a fact that while 
incidence of poverty from 1977-78 to 1999-2000 declined from 51.3%to 
26.1%the decline in number of persons below poverty line in absolute terms 
was not so marked having come down from 328.9 million to 260.2 million. 
 
178 

[5 May, 2005]  RAJYA SABHA 
(b) The Planning Commission uses a Poverty Line based on per capita 
consumption expenditure needed to attain a minimum amount of calorie 
intake out of food consumption along with a minimum amount of non-food 
expenditure in order to meet the requirements of clothing, shelter transport 
etc. 
The Planning Commission, in 1977, constituted a Task Force on 
Projections of Minimum Needs and Effective Consumption Demand, which 
submitted its report in 1979. The Task Force (1979) defined the poverty line 
as per capita consumption expenditure level, which meets the average per 
capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas and 2100 kcal in 
urban areas along with a minimum of non-food expenditure. The Task Force 
used the age-sex-activity specific cal orie allowances recommended by the 
Nutrition Expert Group (1968) to estimate the average daily per capita 
requirement for rural and urban areas using the age-sex-occupational structure 
of their respective population (as projected for 1982-83). Thus, to the extent 
the data permitted, the age, sex and occupational differentials in the daily 
calorie requirement of the population were captured in the average norms. 
The Task Force used the 27th Round (1973-74) NSS data relating to 
household consumption both in quantitative and value terms in order to 
compute the monetary equivalent of these calorie norms, which is known as 
the poverty line. Based on the observed consumer behaviour in 1973-74 it 
was estimated that, on an average, consumer expenditure of Rs. 49.09 per 
capita per month meets the calorie requir ement of 2400 kcal per capita per 
day in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per capita per month with an intake of 21m) 
kcal per capita per day in urban areas. Thus, the concept of poverty line used 
here was partly normative and partly behavioural. 
The present method used by the Planning Commission for estimation of 
poverty is based on the methodology recommended by the Expert Group on 
'Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor' (Lakdawala Committee). The 
Expert Group, which was constituted in September, 1989 submitted its 
Report to the Planning Commission in July, 1993. A full Planning 
Commission meeting chaired by the Prime Minister in March, 1997 accepted 
the recommendations of the Expert Group with minor modifications. Since 
then the estimates of poverty at national and state level are being made using 
the expert Group methodology. According to this Methodology, Planning 
Commission 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
estimates poverty at national and state level from the large sample survey on 
Household Consumer Expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organisation (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five years. The latest 
such survey was conducted in 1999-2000 (NSS 55th round). The Expert 
Group did not redefine the poverty line and adopted the one defined by the 
Task force, which was at national level in rural and urban areas. The Expert 
Group estimated separate poverty lines  for each state by disaggregating the 
national level poverty line. 
The important points of departure between the Expert Group and the 
Task Force methodolgy are: 
(i) Giving up adjustments of the NSS data. A high level of adjustment of 
a survey data distorts its basic characteristic. The difference in the 
level of poverty between the Expert Group and Task Force is largely 
due to the adjustment factor. 
(ii) The Expert Group uses state- specific poverty lines as against a 
national poverty line for rural and urban areas. 
(iii) The Expert Group suggested use of state-specific cost of living 
indices for estimating and updating the poverty line separately for 
rural and urban areas. The Task Force estimates are based on one 
national index, which is same for all the states and also for rural and 
urban areas. The Expert group methodology uses state-wise 
Consumer Price Index of agricultural Labourers (CPIAL) for 
estimating and updating the rural poverty line and Consumer Price 
Index of Industrial workers (CPIIW) for estimating and updating 
urban poverty line. The Government has adopted the Expert Group 
methodology for poverty estimation since March, 1997 as the basis 
for computing the official estimates of poverty in India. 
The decadal growth rate of population has come down from 23.87 in

Census Report.

Transhipment container terminal at Kochi Port 
4607. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: W ill the Minister of SHIPPING, 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a)whether it is a fact that Government have approved the setting up of 
International Transhipment container terminal at Kochi port; 
(b)whether this project has been given to some foreign agency; 
(c) if so, the terms of agreement with this agency; 
(d)to what extent it would be more economical and fast in handling the 
additional traffic; 
(e)whether such a port is also proposed to be set up somewhere on the 
East Coast to upgrade haulage capacity; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The project has been awarded to M/s Dubai Port 
International, UAE, Dubai (DPI) on Build, Operate and Transfer (BOT) basis. 
Licence Agreement has been signed between Cochin Port Trust & M/s India 
Gateway Terminal Private Limited, a subsidiary of DPI, for operation and 
management of Rajiv Gandhi Container Terminal (RGCT) and development 
and operation of International Container Transhipment Terminal (ICTT) on 
31.1.2005. As per provisions of Agreement, the BOT operator is required to 
initially take over the existing Rajiv Gandhi Container Terminal (RGCT) on 
Wellingdon Island, alongwith all the equipments, for operation till the ICTT 
becomes operational. The necessary modernization and augmentation of the 
facilities at RGCT as per the traffic requirement are to be done by the 
Licensee. The new terminal at Vallarpadam is to be commissioned within 4 
years from the date of handing over of  RGCT to the BOT operator. The Port 
Trust is obliged to provide the rail connectivity and National Highway (NH) 
connectivity to the ICTT project site before the new terminal is 
operationalised. However, the BOT operator is obliged to commence the 
construction of the new terminal only on fulfilment of certain Conditions 
Precedent by the Port Trust like ob taining environmental clearance and 
special economic zone status for the project 
203 

RAJYA SABHA  [5 May, 2005] 
area, commencement of construction of rail and NH connectivity to the 
project site. If the construction work s at ICTT have not commenced by the 
date of expiry of six years from the Date of Commercial Operation at RGCT 
on account of non-fulfilment of the Conditions Precedent, either Party is 
entitled to terminate the Agreement, unless otherwise agreed by both the 
parties. 
(d) A large number of containers with origin from or destination to 
India which are presently transshipped through foreign ports mainly at 
Colombo, Salah and Singapore can be handled through this Transhipment 
Terminal, which would result in savings to the tune of Rs, 6,000-16,000 per 
container to the Indian importers and exporters as the transhipment at third 
country ports are avoided. The savings would make Indian export more 
competitive and will boost the export tr ade which will in turn increase the 
demand for products and result in expansion of industries. The savings in the 
transhipment cost and handling costs at the transhipment port will reduce the 
outflow of foreign exchange currently being incurred by the Indian economy. 
Also the cargo carrying capacity of Indian Railways and Konkan Railways 
and National Highways can be economically utilized since a substantial 
volume of ICTT bound containers will choose land mode transportation due 
to convenience and economy vis-a-vis feedering option. With the 
establishment of ICTT, it is expected th at the port traffic will increase from 
14 to 46 million tonnes over the next 10 years period. Direct shipment also 
result in saving in time. 
(e) and (0 The Government has given in-principle approval for the 
setting up of second container terminal  each at Chennai & Tuticorin ports. 
Ennore Port has also planned to set up a new container terminal.

Statement-I 
Criteria for Declaration of National Highways 
1. Roads which run through the length and breadth of the country. 
2. Roads connecting adjacent countries. 
3. Roads connecting the National Capital with State Capital and roads 
connecting mutually the State Capitals. 
4. Roads connecting major ports, larg e industrial centres or tourist 
centers. 
5. Roads meeting very important strategic requirements. 
6. Arterial roads which enable sizeable  reduction in travel distance and 
achieve substantial economic growth thereby. 
7. Roads which held opening up large tracts of backward area and hilly 
regions. 
8. National Highways grid of 100 Km is achieved. 
9. The road must be up to the standard laid down for State Highways—
both in Its technical requirements well as the land requirements. 
 
10. The road and right of way must be free of any type of encroachment 
and should be the property of the State Government. 
11. The right of way required for the National Highways (preferably 
45m, minimum 30m) must be available for acquiring, free of 
encroachments and the State Government would complete acquiring 
formalities within six months.

crashes involving vehicles, while in low and middle income countries, the 
two wheelers, pedestrians and cyclists are at a high risk on this account.

† 4630. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a  fact that consequent upon Government's membership 
in WTO and implementation of patent and present VAT

system, Small and Cottage industries including many tiny units of production 
in the country would be adversely affected and endanger their existence; and 
(b) if so, the details of the efforts being made by Government to save

THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHABIR PRASAD): (a) and (b) India's membership of the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO), amendments to the Patents Act, 1970 and 
implementation of the Value Added Tax (VAT) system are not likely to affect

liberalization/globalization which, inter-alia, include assistance for 
technology/upgradation, common infrastructure development and marketing 
through schemes of cluster development, facilitating availability of 
institutional credit, assistance for adoption of modern management practices, 
use of information technology, etc.

Survey of NSSO 
4632. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will th e Minister of STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the recently released survey of 
the National Sample Survey Organisation on "Household Consumer 
Expenditure and Employment Unemployment Situation" highlighting inter-
alia that three out of every 1000 rural households and one urban household 
per thousand do not get enough to eat in any month of the year; and 
(b) if so, the details of major conclusions/observations contained in the 
survey and action taken/proposed to be taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): 
(a) As per the recently released reports of NSSO Survey on "Household 
Consumer Expenditure and Employment Unemployment" based on NSS 59th 
round conducted during January-Decembe r 2003; at the all-India level the 
proportion of chronically hungry households (not getting enough to eat even 
in any month of the year) was 3 per 1000 for rural areas and 1 per 1000 for 
urban areas. 
The Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution is 
implementing two schemes viz. (i) Targeted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS) and (ii) Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) with a focus on the poor and 
Below Poverty Line (BPL) families:— 
(i) Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) 
Department of Food and Public Distribution introduced the TPDS with 
effect from June 1997 with focus on the poor as a commitment of the 
Government to ensure food security for all, create a hunger free India and 
reform and improve the Public Distribution System (PDS) in order to serve 
the poorest of the poor in the country. 
230 

[5 May, 2005]  RAJYA SABHA 
The scale of issue, which was 10 kg. per family per month for Below 
Poverty Line Families (BPL), was progressively increased.to 20 kg. from 
April, 2000, then to 25 kg. per family per month from July, 2001 and has 
been further increased to 35 kg. per family per month w.e.f. 1st April, 2002. 
The PDS is supplemental in nature and does not envisage meeting the full 
requirements of foodgrains of particular individuals/families. 
(ii) Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) 
AAY was launched in December 2000 . It contemplated identification 
of 1 crore families (out of BPL familie s) who would be provided foodgrains 
@25 kg. per family per month at a more subsidized price of Rs. 2.00 per kg. 
for wheat and Rs. 3.00 per kg. for rice.  The scale of issue has since been 
increased from 25 kg per family per month to 35 kg. per family per month 
w.e.f. 1st April, 2002. The AAY Scheme is being successfully implemented 
in all the States and UTs. The Scheme has been expanded in the year 2003 by 
adding another 50 lakh BPL families. The Scheme has been further expanded 
w.-e.f. 1st August, 2004 by another 50 lakh BPL families by including, inter 
alia, all households at the risk of hunger thus increasing its coverage to 2 
crore BPL household. As announced in the Union Budget 2005-06 the AAY 
is to be expanded to cover another 50 lakh BPL families. 
(b) The major conclusions/observations  contained in the survey are as 
under: - 
* During the survey period Janua ry-December 2003, the all-India 
average monthly per capita consumer expenditure (MPCE) was Rs. 
554 for rural India and Rs. 1022 for urban India. Thus, average 
urban MPCE exceeded average rural MPCE by 84%. 
* in 2003, one-half of the rural population of India had MPCE below 
Rs. 470. About 13% had MPCE below Rs. 300. Among the urban 
population, 80% had MPCE above Rs. 500. About 16% had MPCE 
above Rs. 1500. 
* For rural India, average MPCE of Rs. 554 comprised Rs. 299 for 
food and Rs. 255 for non-food. Food expenditure included Rs. 99 for 
cereals and cereal substitutes and Rs. 105 for milk, milk products, 
vegetables and edible oil. Non-food expenditure included Rs. 51 for 
fuel and light, and Rs. 44 for clothing and footwear. 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
* For the urban population, average MPCE of Rs. 1022 comprised Rs. 
429 for food and Rs. 593 for non-food. Of food expenditure, only 
Rs. 102 went towards cereals' and cereal substitutes while Rs. 161 
was spent on milk, milk products, vegetables and edible oil. Rs. 94 
was spent per person per month on fuel and light, and Rs. 71 on 
clothing and footwear. 
* The share of cereals in total consumption expenditure was 18%-in 
rural India in 2003 compared to 26% in 1987-88. In urban India it 
was 10% in 2003 compared to 15% in 1987-88. 
* The decline in the shar e of food in total expenditure seen over the 
past several rounds continued. The share of food was 54% in rural 
areas compared to 64% in 19 87-88 and 42% in urban areas 
compared to 56% during 1987-88.

4639. SHRI N. R. GOVINDRAJAR: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the funds allocated for sporting events of Indian 
Origin (Kabaddi, Kho-Kho, etc.) during the last three years, State-wise; 
(b) whether traditional sports of Indian origin are vanishing gradually as 
they are not given priority and encouragement; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether Government propose to provide opportunities to rural 
sports persons at national and international level by setting up village sports 
academy and providing them training and other facilities? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI 
SUNIL DUTT): (a) 'Sports' is a State subject and promotion of Sports at the 
State level is the responsibility of the concerned State Government. National 
Sports Federations are also responsible to promote sports at national and 
international level. However, Government during the last three years 
sanctioned Rs. 1.92 crores to recognized National Sports Federations dealing 
the discipline of Indian origin such as Atya Pattya, Carrom, Kabaddi and 
Kho-Kho. However, these funds are no t allocated State-wise. Besides the 
sports tournaments are organized in the discipline of Kho-Kho and Kabaddi 
under the rural Sports Programme. The details of financial assistance released 
to different States/UTs for organizing  competitions in Kabaddi and Kho-Kho 
at district and State level under Rural Sports Programme during the last three 
years is given in the Statement (See below). 
(b) and (c) No, Sir. India won Gold Medals in Kabaddi in Asian 
Games, 1994, 1998 and 2002. Similarly India won a Gold Medal in Kabaddi 
in World Championship held in 2004. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2005] 
(d) The recognized National Sports Federations dealing with 
disciplines of Indian origin and spor ting events of rural base are being 
provided financial assistance as per provisions of the Scheme of Assistance to 
National Sports Federation. Besides, under the Rural Sports Programme rural 
sports tournaments are organized at block, district, state and national levels. 
With a view to spotting and nurturing talented children in sub-junior/ 
junior/senior age groups for achieving excellence at the national/international 
level following schemes are being implemented by Sports Authority of 
India:- 
(i) National Sports Talent Contest Scheme (ii) Army Boys Sports 
Company Scheme (iii) Scheme of SAI Training Centres (iv) Special Area 
Games Scheme (v) Centre of Excellence 
The above Schemes are available to rural sportspersons as well.

The Finance Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI  P. CHIDAMBARAM): Sir, I

"That the Bill to give effect to t he financial proposals of the Central

be taken into consideration". 
Sir, I am grateful to the hon. members who approved and passed the 
Appropriation Bill. The Finance Bill, as  the hon. Members know, is intended to 
give effect to the taxation proposals. So, let me briefly give you the philosophy 
behind the changes that are made in the Finance Bill to the tax laws. 
The Direct Tax side, the previous Government had appointed the 
Kelkar Committee. And, the Task Force of the Kelkar Committee made very 
extensive and valuable recommendations. We have applied our mind, and we 
have accepted some of the more importa nt recommendations. The idea is that 
in direct taxes, there must be a reasonable exemption threshold and then there 
must be reasonable incentive for savings. Taxation has two objectives. One is 
to raise revenue, and the other is to encourage people to save. By appropriate 
rates of taxation, you collect revenue'; by appropriate, incentives and 
exemptions, you encourage people to sa ve. So, the Government decided that 
we will raise the threshold limit to ever yone to one lakh of rupees and we will 
encourage everyone to save, and if they save up to one lakh of rupees that 
also will not be subject to any tax. Ther e is another method of giving tax relief, 
what is called the tax re bate route. The Kelkar Committee has frowned upon 
this route. In my view also, this is not what modern tax systems follow. If you 
go through the tax rebate route,  the State is indicating its bias in favour of one 
instrument as against another instrument. I think, savers are wise people. They 
know what they should save in, whether they should save in instrument 'A' or 
instrument 'B' is a  matter that should be left to the saver. The Government 
should not indicate its bias in favour of  one kind of saving or another kind of 
saving. For example, one saver may think that the National Saving Certificate 
is a good saving instrument; another ma n may think that the LIC insurance 
policy is a better one; the third person may think that the Public Provident Fund 
is a better one. We must leave it to them. Therefore, we cleaned up the whole 
direct taxes side -one lakh exemption across the board; one lakh saving 
268 

[5 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
limit, which will not be taxed. For women, of course, we have a special corner. 
Therefore, we had initially announced one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees, 
but then, when I found that there wa s an anomaly in a small range, we 
immediately corrected that anomaly, and,  now, we have made it one lakh 
thirty-five thousand rupees. For senior citizens, again, we have a special 
corner. We initially announced one lakh fifty thousand rupees. But, when I 
found that the pensioner senior citizen, not the non-pensioner senior citizen, 
the pensioner senior citizen's pension is reckoned as salary for the purpose of

one bracket, we made it one lakh eighty -five thousand rupees. Sir, there is a

SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR (Punjab): Madam, I rise to support the Finance 
Bill, 2005, presented by the Finance Mini ster. Madam, before I dwell upon the 
specifics of my intervention, I would like to spell out what I consider to be the 
measure by which the Bill is to be tested.  Madam, in my reading of the Bill, it 
seeks to achieve the twin objectives of  putting the fiscal administration of the 
country into a straighter jacket, and it se eks, at the same time, to ensure a much 
enlarged tax base and also an equitable distribution of the tax burden. It also 
seeks, in my understanding of the Bill,  to meet the challenge of unaccounted 
wealth, which by some accounts is a parallel economy in this country, and is not 
being put to productive uses and thereby is a great threat to the overarching 
public and national interest. 
I think, Madam, the Bill seeks to do yet another social obligation. It 
seeks to ensure a simpler tax administrat ion, a credible tax bracket structure 
and, overall, a discernible transparency in the administration of the taxation 
regime. I think, viewed in this perspective, the Finance Minister was called upon 
to make certain choices. No w, it cannot be anybody's case that all the choices 
are always perfect, and that the other view is not a possible view to take. I do 
believe that there is another perspective which has been expressed by some of 
my esteemed colleagues. Two views are possible. But in the overall intent, I can 
scarcely find a flaw with the underlining philosophical basis of the Bill. It is a fact 
that unaccounted wealth is routed through the banking system. There can be no 
two views about it. It is a fact, and two cases have been pointed out in debates 
in the Lok Sabha that within less than two months, Rs. 110 crores were 
deposited in a single bank account in cash and about Rs. 38 crores were 
withdrawn in cash from that bank account. There are any number of such 
instances. We know that the banking system in this country has been abused  
and misused.  Therefore, it was necessary to have some kind of a

SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY (Pondicherry): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, 
I rise to support this Bill. 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN:  What is there in this small Bill? 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Sir, there are so many things in this Bill 
on which I would like to speak. Thank you very much for giving me an 
opportunity to speak on the Government of Union Territories and the 
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) pill, 2005. 
351 

RAJYA SABHA  [5 May, 2005] 
Though the amendment is very sma ll, the hon. Minister has brought 
forward this amending Bill for th e purpose of delimitation of the 
constituencies in the Union Territory of Pondicherry and in the National 
Capital Territory of Delhi. At some  places, we have State Legislatures 
and at some places we have Union Territories Administration. Sir, 
through this Bill, the hon. Minister  wants to amend Section 3 of the 
Government of Union Territories Act, 1963. In Section 3, it is said, "For 
the figures "2000", the figures "2026" shall be substituted; and for the 
figures "1971", the figures "2001" sh all be substituted." And, it will 
make corresponding changes in the Government of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 also. Sir, the peculiar part of it is that the 
NDA Government was in power when the Delimitation Act was brought 
in the Parliament, and it was passed without discussion in the Lok 
Sabha. Within fifteen minutes, the Bill was approved by the House. 
Now, the situation is such that we find so many lacunae in the 
delimitation of constituencies, whether in the urban areas or in the rural 
areas. Most of the States are now fi nding it difficult to cope with the 
guidelines that had been issued by the Delimitation Commission. 
Sir, take the case of some of the urban areas. Now, there is lot 
of migration taking place. People who lived in the rural areas have 
come to the cities. Take the case of Bangalore. In the urban and semi-
urban areas of Bangalore, the constituencies numbered about 21 in 
rural areas and about nine to ten in the urban areas. Now, according to 
the population, it should come to nearly 35 constituencies. 
I want the hon. Minister to consider this. In the rural areas, the 
number of constituencies is being reduced because there is a thin 
population in those areas. While appl ying the criterion of population, 
the number of constituencies in rural areas is being reduced, and it is 
being increased in the urban areas. When we apply the same 
yardstick for all the States, there is a hue and cry from the people 
living in the rural areas. The political parties, voluntary organizations, 
and some of the associations, all of them made representations to the 
Delimitation Commission. 
Sir, the Delimitation Commission follows certain procedures. 
They prepare the blue-print, they draft a proposal, give it to Members, 
and they have got to be associatedby  Members of the Legislature and 
elected Members of Parliament, who have no voting rights. In the 
Committee, we have no voting rights. Only three members have the 
voting rights -- the Chairman of the Commission, one member from the 
Section Commission, and thirdly, the State Election Commissioner. 
The views of the other 
352 

[5 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
Members are heard and ignored. This is something that I have seen in my 
State. I would like to tell the hon. Minist er for Home Affairs that in the Union 
Territory of Pondicherry, where delimit ation was done, there are 21 assembly 
constituencies in Pondicherry -- six assembly constituencies in Karaikkal, two 
assembly constituencies in Mahe, and one assembly constituency in  Yanam. I 
would like to say for the information of the hon. Minister that Pondicherry is the 
State Capital, Karaikkal is about 135 k ilometres from Pondicherry, near Tamil 
Nadu, the Mahe region is about 600 kilometres from Pondicherry, and Yanam 
is about-700 kilometres from Pondicherry. The Regional Administrators are 
taking care of the administration there. The elected represent atives from that 
area are assisting, the people by introducing welfare schemes there. 
Now, only the criterion of populati on is adopted. In Karaikkal, which 
has six assembly segments, they are reducing one constituency because 
they effected population control. Sir, there is a punishment for the region 
where they are effecting population c ontrol; they reduced the number of 
constituencies by one! The Delimitation Commission went there; people made 
a representation to them; all the politic al parties said unanimously that the 
number of constituencies should not be reduced, but they have decided that 
they would provide only for five constituencies. 
Sir, the Mahe region is a very sens itive region, which is on the Kerala 
border. There they have effectively im plemented population control. But there 
they have reduced the number of constituencies to one. What will happen to 
the elected representatives? What will happen to the public? There is a hue 
and cry over the issue; there is a revol t. The hon. Minister should understand 
that it is not a contiguous  area; the area is distributed in four places. One area 
is in Kerala, one is in Andhra Pradesh, and two regions are near Tamil Nadu. 
The hon. Deputy Chairman also visited t hose places when those regions were 
affected by the tsunami. People's s entiments need to be understood. We 
should not only go by the rules. P eople made unanimous representations. As 
political parties and as Members of Parliament, we also made representations. 
They fixed the  population criteria. They increased the constituencies in 
Pondicherry region by two seats by reducing two seats in the other region. By 
doing that, they brought the average population. The average, which they gave 
in Pondicherry, is equally applicable for six seats in Karaikal region. But they 
have not heard our grievances simply because the Delimitation Commission is 
directly answerable to the hon. President of India. They simply heard the

views of the political parties, and the public opinion was ignored.   I will very 
categorically say that they ignored the public opinion. 
Sir, there is another lacuna in this  Bill which I want the hon. Minister 
to clarify. Sir, the amendment has b een brought after the completion of 
delimitation -- hon. Minister is putting the cart before the horse. Why didn't they 
bring the amendment earlier? After the amendment, the delimitation work 
should have been started. According to the Union Territories Act, the First 
Amendment has been brought in 19 71, and then the de limitation of 
constituencies was done. Before doing the delimitation of the constituencies,

Minister has brought the amendment a fter the delimitation work has been 
done. I want to know the response of the hon. Minister on this. After 
completing the delimitation work, you are coming with amendment as a 
formality. They should tell us that they are doing it as per the Delimitation Act 
of 2001. There is another legal angle. In the Union Territories Act, whether it is 
Delhi or Pondicherry, there is a sp ecial provision for delimitation of 
constituency. From Section 3 to Section 9 of the Union Territories Act, 1963, it 
has been mentioned how the constituencies have to be delimited. It is also 
mentioned in the Delhi Act. This is a special law for the Union Territories. But 
that is a general law for delimitation. Which law will be applicable? I want to 
know that from the hon. Minister. He has to answer this legal angle also 
because tomorrow if somebody goes to Court, the Government of India has to 
answer that point.

have powers of the States. When they wa nt the Statehood, it is not being 
given. We have been demanding that the Union Territory of Pondicherry

Assembly of Pondicherry passed a unanimo us Resolution, all political parties

are limited. The Chief Minister's decision and the Cabinet decision can be 
vetoed by the Lt. Governor. The powers vested with the elected 
representatives can be diluted by the Lt. Governor.
